info.what: The app or browser a person uses to talk to your system.
info.why: Every interaction starts here: opening a page, tapping a button or sending a message becomes a request to your servers.
info.analogy: A customer walking up to a shop counter.

samples.caption: The request a browser sends to open an order
samples.code:
GET /orders/101 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci…

samples.caption: …and the response it gets back

info.what: Turns a name like example.com into the numeric address of a server.
info.why: People remember names; computers connect to IP addresses. DNS can also send each user to the nearest or healthiest server.
info.analogy: The internet's phone book.

samples.caption: Records for shop.example.com
Looking a name up from a terminal
samples.code:
$ dig +short shop.example.com
203.0.113.10

info.what: A network of servers around the world that keeps copies of your files close to users.
info.why: Images, videos and scripts load much faster from nearby, and your own servers handle far less traffic.
info.analogy: Local warehouses stocking popular items so deliveries arrive quickly.

samples.caption: A nearby copy answers: the origin never sees it
samples.code:
GET /images/logo.png
Host: cdn.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=86400
X-Cache: HIT
Age: 3150

samples.caption: How long each file is kept: versioned names can stay a year, personal data never

info.what: A service run by another company that your system calls over the internet.
info.why: Some jobs, like taking payments or sending email, are hard to build and run well. Renting them is faster and often safer.
info.analogy: Hiring a courier instead of buying your own delivery vans.

samples.caption: Charging a card through a payment provider's API
When it's done, they call you back (a webhook)

info.what: Spreads incoming requests across several identical servers.
info.why: No single server gets overwhelmed, and if one breaks, traffic simply goes to the others.
info.analogy: A restaurant host seating guests at different tables.

samples.caption: NGINX spreading requests over three servers (round-robin by default)
Round-robin: each request goes to the next server

info.what: The single front door to all your backend services.
info.why: It checks who is calling, applies shared rules like rate limits, and forwards each request to the right service, so every service doesn't have to do it.
info.analogy: A hotel reception that checks guests in and points them to the right room.

samples.caption: Routes: which service handles which path
The same rule written as configuration
samples.code:
routes:
  - path: /orders/*
    service: orders-service
    auth: jwt
    rateLimit: 100/minute

info.what: Caps how many requests someone can make in a period of time.
info.why: Protects the system from abuse and from buggy clients that send too much, and keeps things fair between users.
info.analogy: A bouncer letting in a set number of people per minute.

samples.caption: Token bucket: 5 requests per second per user
What a rejected client receives
samples.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 1
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

info.what: Keeps a live, two-way connection open with each user.
info.why: The server can push new messages or updates the moment they happen, instead of waiting for the user to ask.
info.analogy: An open phone line instead of letters sent back and forth.

samples.caption: The browser opens one connection and keeps it
Who is connected where

info.what: Knows which part of a split-up database holds each piece of data, and sends queries there.
info.why: When data is too big for one machine it is split into shards. The router hides that split, so the app talks to it as if it were one database.
info.analogy: A library catalogue telling you which building holds a book.

samples.caption: Shard map: users split by id range
Hash routing: the same key always lands on the same shard

info.what: Runs your application's code: the business logic.
info.why: It receives a request, applies your rules (log in, place an order), talks to databases and other services, and sends back the answer.
info.analogy: The kitchen that actually prepares the meals.

samples.caption: An endpoint: this is where the business rules live
What happens to one request

info.what: Runs background jobs that don't need an immediate answer.
info.why: Slow tasks like sending emails or resizing images happen behind the scenes, so users don't have to wait for them.
info.analogy: Back-office staff finishing paperwork after the customer has left.

samples.caption: A worker takes jobs from a queue, one at a time
Jobs and their state

info.what: A small piece of code that runs only when something triggers it, with no server for you to manage.
info.why: You pay only while it runs, and it scales up and down automatically. Handy for occasional or spiky work.
info.analogy: Calling a taxi when you need one instead of owning a car.

samples.caption: A complete function: runs whenever a file is uploaded
It scales with demand on its own, down to zero

info.what: Stores data in tables of rows and columns, with strict rules about its shape.
info.why: Ideal when data is related (users, orders, payments) and must stay correct: transactions make a group of changes happen completely or not at all.
info.analogy: A well-organised spreadsheet with rules nobody can break.

samples.caption: users
orders: user_id points to a row in users
A query that joins both tables
samples.code:
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM orders
JOIN users ON users.id = orders.user_id
WHERE orders.status = 'paid';

info.what: Stores data in flexible forms, like documents or key–value pairs, without a fixed table layout.
info.why: Spreads easily across many machines and suits huge volumes of simple lookups, or data whose shape changes often.
info.analogy: Labelled folders you can fill with whatever fits.

samples.caption: One document keeps everything about a user together, nested
Fetched by its key, in one step
samples.code: db.users.findOne({ _id: "user_1" })

info.what: Keeps frequently used data in fast memory.
info.why: Answers repeated questions in a fraction of a millisecond and takes load off the database. The trade-off: cached data can be slightly out of date.
info.analogy: Keeping the things you use most on your desk instead of in the archive.

samples.caption: Keys and values, each with an expiry time
Check the cache first; on a miss, read the database and keep a copy

info.what: Stores files of any size, like images, videos and backups, which you fetch by name.
info.why: Cheap, practically unlimited and very durable. The right home for big files that don't belong in a database.
info.analogy: A huge self-storage facility where every box has a label.

samples.caption: Each file lives under a key that looks like a path
Files are read and written over HTTP, by key
samples.code:
GET /my-bucket/avatars/ana.png
PUT /my-bucket/videos/42/original.mp4

info.what: Organises text so it can be searched quickly, like a search engine for your own data.
info.why: Databases are slow at "find everything mentioning these words". A search index does it fast and handles typos, ranking and filters.
info.analogy: The index at the back of a book.

samples.caption: An inverted index: each word points to the documents that contain it
A search: matches words in any order, best hits first

info.what: Holds tasks in line until a worker is ready to take them.
info.why: The app can hand off work and reply right away. If workers are slow or down, tasks wait safely instead of being lost.
info.analogy: Take-a-number tickets at a deli counter.

info.what: Delivers each message to everyone who subscribed to a topic.
info.why: Senders don't need to know who is listening, and new listeners can join without changing the sender.
info.analogy: A radio station: everyone tuned in hears the broadcast.

info.what: An ordered, durable log of events that many readers can process, and replay, at their own pace.
info.why: Suits high volumes of events (clicks, payments, sensor readings) that several systems need to handle, now or later.
info.analogy: A recorded TV channel you can rewind.

info.what: Collects what every service writes down and makes it searchable in one place.
info.why: When something goes wrong you can read exactly what happened, across all servers, instead of logging into each machine one by one.
info.analogy: A ship's logbook, kept for the whole fleet.

info.what: Records numbers over time, like requests per second, error rate and response time.
info.why: Shows at a glance whether the system is healthy, and reveals trends, like slowly growing response times, before users complain.
info.analogy: The gauges on a car's dashboard.

info.what: Follows a single request as it travels through every service, timing each step.
info.why: With many services involved, it shows exactly where a slow or failed request got stuck.
info.analogy: A parcel-tracking page showing every stop along the way.

info.what: Watches the metrics and notifies a person when something crosses a limit.
info.why: Problems are noticed and fixed quickly, at any hour, instead of being discovered by customers.
info.analogy: A smoke alarm.

info.what: Catches crashes and exceptions, groups identical ones and shows the code that failed.
info.why: Turns thousands of scattered error messages into a short list of bugs, ranked by how many users they affect.
info.analogy: A mechanic's fault report listing each problem and how often it happens.
